lines.text: What lifts a drink up a straw? Surprisingly, not suction.
lines.phonemes: wˌʌt lˈɪfts ɐ dɹˈɪŋk ˌʌp ɐ stɹˈɔː? sɚpɹˈaɪzɪŋli, nˌɑːt sˈʌkʃən.

lines.text: A glass of water. A straw. One sip. The water climbs twenty centimeters, to your lips. It feels like you're pulling it.
lines.phonemes: ɐ ɡlˈæs ʌv wˈɔːɾɚ. ɐ stɹˈɔː. wˈʌn sˈɪp. ðə wˈɔːɾɚ klˈaɪmz twˈɛnti sˈɛntɪmˌiːɾɚz, tə jʊɹ lˈɪps. ɪt fˈiːlz lˈaɪk jʊɹ pˈʊlɪŋ ɪt.

lines.text: Now fill it completely. Seal it, airtight, with a lid. Then sip, as hard as possible. Nothing rises.
lines.phonemes: nˈaʊ fˈɪl ɪt kəmplˈiːtli. sˈiːl ɪt, ˈɛɹtaɪt, wɪð ɐ lˈɪd. ðˈɛn sˈɪp, æz hˈɑːɹd æz pˈɑːsᵻbəl. nˈʌθɪŋ ɹˈaɪzᵻz.

lines.text: In sixteen forty-four, Torricelli saw why. We live at the bottom of an ocean of air, and it presses on everything. A sip lowers the pressure inside the straw, and the air outside pushes the drink up. How hard can it push?
lines.phonemes: ɪn sˈɪkstiːn fˈɔːɹɾifˈɔːɹ, tˌɔɹəʧˈɛli sˈɔː wˈaɪ. wiː lˈɪv æt ðə bˈɑːɾəm əvən ˈoʊʃən ʌv ˈɛɹ, ænd ɪt pɹˈɛsᵻz ˌɔn ˈɛvɹɪθˌɪŋ. ɐ sˈɪp lˈoʊɚz ðə pɹˈɛʃɚɹ ɪnsˈaɪd ðə stɹˈɔː, ænd ðɪ ˈɛɹ aʊtsˈaɪd pˈʊʃᵻz ðə dɹˈɪŋk ˈʌp. hˌaʊ hˈɑːɹd kæn ɪt pˈʊʃ?

lines.text: Make the straw three stories tall. Your lungs? About one meter. With a perfect pump, the water stops near ten meters. At the top, room-temperature water boils.
lines.phonemes: mˌeɪk ðə stɹˈɔː θɹˈiː stˈɔːɹiz tˈɔːl. jʊɹ lˈʌŋz? ɐbˌaʊt wˈʌn mˈiːɾɚ. wɪð ɐ pˈɜːfɛkt pˈʌmp, ðə wˈɔːɾɚ stˈɑːps nˌɪɹ tˈɛn mˈiːɾɚz. æt ðə tˈɑːp, ɹˈuːmtˈɛmpɹɪtʃɚ wˈɔːɾɚ bˈɔɪlz.

lines.text: Measure it: the air above one square centimeter weighs just over a kilogram. So does ten point three meters of water.
lines.phonemes: mˈɛʒɚɹ ɪt: ðɪ ˈɛɹ əbˌʌv wˈʌn skwˈɛɹ sˈɛntɪmˌiːɾɚ wˈeɪz dʒˈʌst ˌoʊvɚɹ ɐ kˈɪləɡɹˌæm. sˌoʊ dˈʌz tˈɛn pˈɔɪnt θɹˈiː mˈiːɾɚz ʌv wˈɔːɾɚ.

lines.text: Straws don't pull. You thin the air inside, and the atmosphere pushes.
lines.phonemes: stɹˈɔːz dˈoʊnt pˈʊl. juː θˈɪn ðɪ ˈɛɹ ɪnsˈaɪd, ænd ðɪ ˈætməsfˌɪɹ pˈʊʃᵻz.
